stemMd: A single nucleotide is inserted near the beginning of a protein-coding sequence, outside any intron. Which consequence is most likely unless another mutation compensates?

options.label: A
options.textMd: No possible change to downstream amino acids

options.label: B
options.textMd: A mandatory doubling of chromosome number

options.label: C
options.textMd: A shift in the reading frame for downstream codons

options.label: D
options.textMd: Loss of exactly one amino acid with all later codons unchanged

options.label: E
options.textMd: Conversion of every chromosome into RNA

explanationMd: Codons are read in consecutive groups of three. Inserting a number of bases not divisible by three changes the grouping downstream, often altering many amino acids and introducing an early stop codon. An insertion of three bases would have a different, in-frame effect.

distractorRationale.a: One inserted base changes how subsequent triplets are grouped.
distractorRationale.d: An insertion of one base is not an in-frame deletion of a triplet.
distractorRationale.e: The mutation changes one sequence, not the chemical identity of all chromosomes.
distractorRationale.b: A point insertion does not cause polyploidy.
